title: Death through Adam, Life through Christ
english: …by the old charges, and our sin is not washed away. In vain, too, did the inspired singer say, “Lord, you were pleased with your land; you forgave your people their iniquities; you covered all their sins” (Psalm 85:1–2); and again, “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not reckon sin” (Psalm 32:1–2). And yet the blessed Paul says, in his Letter to the Romans, that the blessing spoken in these words reaches both the circumcision and those from the Gentiles (Romans 4:9). For we have been justified in Christ, “who was handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25).

“Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished” (1 Corinthians 15:18). For it seems they have been deceived and have laid down their lives for him without reward, if Christ has not been raised. If the hope of the saints is not full of immortality, if they do not look to reign with him, then perhaps they have perished; and since they endured even death itself for nothing of use, their labors have brought them only loss. Away with such dreadful ignorance! For “the dead shall rise, and those in the tombs shall be raised,” as the prophet says (Isaiah 26:19); and he who hands out the crowns weighs out to each the one most fitting for him, and he will surely bring punishment on the ungodly; for as God he is the judge of all.

“But now Christ has been raised from the dead, and has become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,” and so on (1 Corinthians 15:20). From here he takes it as agreed that we must believe that Christ came to life again and became the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, the first of those on earth to trample down death, just as our forefather Adam was the first to step into it and became the firstfruits of those who slipped into corruption. And that the resurrection of the dead will follow the resurrection of our Savior he adds when he says, “For as death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead also came through a man” (1 Corinthians 15:21).

See how he shows once more that the mystery of the dispensation in the flesh is full of a skill worthy of God. For it was needful, truly needful, he says, that a man should conquer death for us. For this reason God the Word, who shone forth from God, did not take hold of angels, as Paul himself says, but of the seed of Abraham, so that he might be made like his brothers in every way (Hebrews 2:16–17). For, as I said, what had fallen sick had to be healed, and what had fallen had to rise. What had come under death through transgression and sin had to overcome death through obedience and righteousness. That is why the Only-begotten Word of God, who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21), became man: so that, as in Adam we have all been condemned, when human nature suffered death, so also, justified in Christ, we might strip off, together with sin, the death that sprang from it. The inspired Paul himself will bear witness, saying, “For as by the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners” (Romans 5:19).

So, as in Adam all die (1 Corinthians 15:22), since, as I said, human nature was condemned in him because of the transgression, so in Christ they will be made alive, since in him human nature is blessed again in the same way because of the justification. The second, then, is the undoing of the first. For “he was handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25). So when he was raised, we too were raised with him. For the Word who is from God is Life by nature; and he surely does not give the good that belongs to his nature, I mean life, to his own flesh alone, but passes it on to the whole of human nature.

Christ, as all agree, has been raised as the firstfruits, “so that he himself might have first place in all things” (Colossians 1:18), as it is written. Yet in due time the others will follow in coming to life again, though, as is fitting, not in a confused mass, but in order, rank by rank, and as at a word of command (compare 1 Thessalonians 4:16). For after the firstfruits, that is, Christ, he says, those who are his will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:23). Clearly he means those who belong to the time…

title: The Son Hands Over the Kingdom
english: …of his coming among us, that is, those who lived after he became man, and who have fallen asleep in faith. For there were, admittedly, saints from time to time in Israel, while the life under the law was praised and still held sway. But those in Christ are better: they have been justified through faith, have become partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4), and have been made rich with the Spirit of adoption (Romans 8:15). They have also been called by grace into brotherhood with him who is Son by nature and in truth. Among those under the law there was a spirit of slavery, but we cry, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15). So, as I said, those in Christ are better than those of older times.

That is why he says that they will be the first to come to life again, following, as it were, in the footsteps of him who is the beginning of all, because they are closer to him and for this reason have been honored above the others. Our Lord Jesus Christ himself also hints at something of this kind in the parables of the Gospel. For he said that the one who hired the workers for the vineyard (he was the master of the house), “when evening came, said to his steward, ‘Call the workers and pay them their wages, beginning from the last up to the first’” (Matthew 20:8).

“Then comes the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he has destroyed every rule and every authority and power” (1 Corinthians 15:24). He says that the kingdom will be handed over by the Son to God the Father when every rule of the unclean spirits has been destroyed and death itself is at last wholly idle.

“When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28). Since some try, as far as lies with them, to belittle the Son, saying that he hands over the kingdom to the Father and is subject to him as to one greater, we must say that the Son underwent the voluntary self-emptying when he became like us, and humbled himself, as it were, from the heights, though he was of the same form as the Father and equal to him (compare Philippians 2:6–8). Now seated at the right hand of the Father, he is hidden in God (compare Colossians 3:3), but he will be revealed in glory at the time of the end of the present age.

If he is brought down from the honor he now has, does he then undergo a second self-emptying? And if he also hands over the kingdom, how does he come “with the holy angels in the glory of his Father” (Mark 8:38)? So it would be unwelcome to the Son that “his enemies should be put under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25), if now he reigns with the Father but then falls from the kingdom. Yet even if the Son is subject to the Father, he is not for that reason less than the Father. For subjection is not a defining mark of nature and essence; it points rather to a way of acting. Even among us, when it happens, it does not show that we are of different essence from one another. How so? A son is subject to a father, a slave to a master, a pupil to a teacher, and one of those under a ruler’s hand and yoke to the ruler. Yet in none of these cases is the principle of sameness of essence harmed; for they are of one kind with one another, even if they stand in this relation, yielding to one another and being subject, and not counting it a dishonor, for the sake of what is beneficial.

How then can they make an argument that is weak even in our case hold good in the case of God? For if, as they say, being subject is a property or measure of nature in the Son, then his not being subject is the property of another nature in him, a nature perhaps better than that one, if subjection belongs to lesser beings. For he is subject by way of the dispensation, for our sake.

The sense of the words is this. Since man sinned and came under corruption, and through the devil and the demons fell away from him who is God by nature, the Only-begotten became man for our sake and destroyed the power of death; he also removed sin, the root of death, and cast out the ruler of this age (compare John 12:31). Having done all this, when the whole dispensation has been brought to completion, he hands over, that is, he will present, to the Father the kingdom that had long ago been plundered and had passed under the power of others…

title: How Are the Dead Raised?
english: …restoring to him authority over all things on earth. When death and Satan, who had tyrannized over them, have been destroyed, the Son will again have, in the age to come as well, supremacy of authority over all things.
Tome Seven.

“But someone will say, ‘How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?’” and so on (1 Corinthians 15:35). The prophet Isaiah cried out long beforehand the mystery of the resurrection from the dead, that it will take place in due time, as God grants it and by his unspeakable power refashions into life what death held fast. He said, “The dead shall rise, and those in the tombs shall be raised, and those in the earth shall rejoice; for the dew that comes from you is healing to them” (Isaiah 26:19). By dew, I think, he means figuratively the life-giving working of God, by which he gives being to things that are not, and grants well-being to things already brought into existence. For all things hold together in him (Colossians 1:17), just as they were also brought into being through him (compare John 1:3).

And somewhere the inspired David sings of the creatures on earth to God, the Savior of all: “When you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness; when you turn away your face, they will be troubled; you will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust; you will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Psalm 104:28–30). For in Adam, because of the transgression, human nature suffered the turning away of the divine face; and so it was all but thrown into confusion and troubled, went back to its own dust, and was brought down into death and corruption. But since the Only-begotten Word of God has become like us, and we have been enriched with a share in the Holy Spirit, we are being reshaped to what we were in the beginning and, as it were, created anew. For we have been called to newness of life (Romans 6:4), escaping the power of death.

The most wise Paul will bear witness, saying, “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will give life to your mortal bodies also through his Spirit who dwells in you” (Romans 8:11). Since, then, Christ came to life again, trampling down the power of death, and became the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, who will surely follow in his footsteps, how is it not utter madness still to doubt the mystery of the resurrection in any way at all?

If anyone chose to turn the eye of his mind too curiously on the works of the Godhead, and tried to look closely into the manner in which each thing was brought forth and the beginning of its coming to be, he would never stop uttering that senseless “How?” For how did the heaven come to be, from what matter, or from where? What foundation does it have? And the earth, how or from where did it come, and on what does it rest firm? How were the orb of the sun, the moon, the stars, and the other created things brought forth? How did the Maker of all take dust from the earth and form man (Genesis 2:7)? How was earth refashioned into bones and sinews and flesh? If, because we shall not be able to give an account of each thing that has been made, we shall for that reason deny that they came to be at all, where would these notions, or rather these perverse arguments, finally end?

After Christ’s resurrection, to doubt the resurrection, to say “How?” of the works of God, is a mark of bad judgment, ignorance, and arrogance. And indeed to ask, “With what body are the dead raised?” is also foolish; for it is quite plain that it is with the same body. For the Lord too raised his own flesh just as it was. But as for those who say that the soul existed beforehand and is bound to the body as a punishment, they set aside not only the account of creation, according to which…
